Clause (79) exempts profit on debt from a rupee account held with a scheduled bank by a person maintaining an NRVA or NRBVA under the SBP scheme, where deposits are made exclusively from foreign exchange remitted into the account. Clause (5AC) of Part II sets the withholding rate on profit on debt covered by (78) and (79) at zero percent.
source: Income Tax Ordinance consolidated to 30 June 2026, Second Schedule Part I cls (78) and (79), Part II cl (5AC)
note: Useful contrast for the guide: this is what an actual exemption looks like in this Ordinance, and s.111(4) is not drafted that way.

claim: The Finance Act 2026 amended clause (79) of Part I of the Second Schedule, replacing the reference to 'non-resident individuals holding POC, NICOP or CNIC' with 'a person maintaining a Non-Resident Pakistani Rupee Value Account (NRVA) or Non-Resident Business Value Account (NRBVA) under the scheme introduced by the State Bank of Pakistan'. The Finance Act 2026 also substituted the words 'Foreign Currency Accounts Scheme' with 'any foreign currency account scheme(s)' in clause (78).
source: Income Tax Ordinance consolidated to 30 June 2026, Second Schedule footnotes; corroborated by KPMG Finance Act 2026 brief
note: Tier 1 and tier 2 agree. KPMG describes the same substitution in its 'Amendments in exemption' section. The eligibility test shifts from what card the person holds to which account they maintain.

claim: Clause (114A) of Part IV of the Second Schedule was SUBSTITUTED by the Finance Act 2026. It disapplies s.114(1)(ae) (the return requirement for persons whose income is subject to final taxation) and s.181 (taxpayer registration / NTN) for a person maintaining an FCVA, FCBVA, NRVA or NRBVA with authorised banks under SBP foreign exchange regulations. The pre-2026 version was limited to a non-resident individual holding POC, NICOP or CNIC maintaining an FCVA or NRVA. A proviso withdraws the relief if the person has Pakistan-source taxable income other than five listed categories: profit on debt on those accounts; profit on debt on GOP securities bought from their proceeds; capital gain on immovable property acquired from FCVA or NRVA proceeds; capital gain on PSX securities and mutual fund units acquired from their proceeds; and dividend income from such securities and funds.
source: Income Tax Ordinance consolidated to 30 June 2026, Second Schedule Part IV cl (114A) and its footnote 4
note: Directly answers the 'do I have to file' question for RDA investors, and note it also switches off s.181 registration. The FA2026 substitution widens the class to the two business value accounts and drops the card-holding requirement from the opening words.

claim: s.152(1DA) was substituted by the Finance Act 2026. It now requires every banking company maintaining an FCVA, FCBVA, NRVA or NRBVA to deduct tax from capital gain arising on disposal of debt instruments and Government securities and certificates invested through those accounts, at the rate in Division II of Part III of the First Schedule. The pre-2026 text applied only to an FCVA or NRVA of a non-resident individual holding POC, NICOP or CNIC. Under s.152(1E) the tax deductible under (1DA) is a FINAL tax.
source: Income Tax Ordinance consolidated to 30 June 2026, s.152(1DA), (1E) and footnote 1
note: Third instance of the same FA2026 pattern: the RDA account family is widened from FCVA/NRVA to include the business value accounts FCBVA and NRBVA, and the POC/NICOP/CNIC gate is dropped. Same pattern in cl (79), cl (111AB) and cl (114A).

claim: Second proviso to s.236C(1): where the seller or transferor is a non-resident individual holding POC, NICOP or CNIC who had acquired the immovable property through an FCVA or NRVA maintained with authorised banks under SBP foreign exchange regulations, the tax collected under s.236C is a final discharge of tax liability in lieu of capital gains taxable under s.37. The mirror proviso to s.236K makes the tax collected a final discharge of tax liability for such a buyer or transferee.
source: Income Tax Ordinance consolidated to 30 June 2026, s.236C(1) second proviso and s.236K proviso
note: CONFIRMS the claim the caller had already verified, now read verbatim from the post-Finance-Act-2026 consolidation, and adds the s.236K buyer-side mirror which the caller did not mention. Note both provisos still carry the POC/NICOP/CNIC wording that FA2026 removed from cl (114A), cl (79), s.152(1DA) and cl (111AB): the widening was not applied uniformly.

claim: Clause (111AB) of Part IV of the Second Schedule: the provisions of s.100BA and rule 1 of the Tenth Schedule shall not apply to FCVA, FCBVA, NRVA or NRBVA accounts with authorised banks under SBP foreign exchange regulations. Clause (111AC) separately disapplies s.100BA and rule 1 of the Tenth Schedule to a non-resident individual holding POC or NICOP in respect of transactions on which tax is collectible under s.236C and s.236K.
source: Income Tax Ordinance consolidated to 30 June 2026, Second Schedule Part IV cls (111AB) and (111AC)
note: Means the non-filer doubling in the Tenth Schedule does not bite on these accounts or, under (111AC), on POC/NICOP holders' property transactions. Pairs with the already-recorded overseas-PSID filer-rate route.

claim: Para 13(II)(D) of Chapter 20 of the SBP Foreign Exchange Manual, as revised by FE Circular No. 01 of 11 July 2024, grants resident INDIVIDUALS general permission for exactly three categories of investment abroad: (1) small investment in shares of LISTED companies abroad, capped at USD 25,000 per calendar year and at 1 percent of the investee company's shares; (2) participation in Employee Stock Option Plans of a foreign parent, capped at USD 50,000 per calendar year and 3 percent of shares; and (3) sweat equity acquired without monetary consideration for the individual's own efforts and services in a field of expertise, capped at 20 percent of shares and requiring the agreement to be submitted to SBP. There is no general permission for a resident individual to incorporate or acquire a private company abroad.
source: SBP FE Circular No. 01 of 2024, Annexure A, Para 13(II)(D), read verbatim from research/raw/sbp-fe2024c1-annexA.pdf
note: THE MOST CONSEQUENTIAL FINDING IN THE CROSS-BORDER CLUSTER. Most Pakistani freelancers who form a US LLC do so PERSONALLY, not through a Pakistani company. The 2024 liberalisation that everyone cites is Para 13(II)A, which applies to export-oriented COMPANIES in the IT sector. Section D, the individual section, was not similarly liberalised and its three routes do not cover forming your own LLC. Note also the reporting duties in Para 13(III): documentary evidence within one month, form V-100 within one month, audited financials of the investee annually, and dividends and disinvestment proceeds repatriated through banking channels with a Proceeds Realization Certificate filed with SBP. State the gap as a gap; do not assert that it is prohibited without a prohibition provision, which was not read.

claim: Para 13(II)(A1)(2) provides three routes for equity investment abroad by export-oriented IT companies: (a) from an Exporter's Special Foreign Currency Account to the extent of funds available, with no prior bank designation; (b) from a Special Foreign Currency Account holding equity raised from abroad, also without designation; and (c) for an IT company not yet exporting or without sufficient ESFCA/SFCA balances, up to the average net profit of the last three financial years or USD 100,000, whichever is higher, after prior designation of an Authorized Dealer. Para 13(II)(A1)(3) conditions apply to all three: total investment abroad must not exceed 80 percent of the company's equity for a non-listed company; the foreign business must be of a similar nature or an extended line of the applicant's Pakistani business; operational expenses of a marketing or liaison office are capped at USD 30,000 annually from the second year with up to 10 percent annual increases; and an unlisted acquisition above USD 1 million needs a valuation report from an accredited firm in the target country.
source: SBP FE Circular No. 01 of 2024, Annexure A, Para 13(II)(A1), read verbatim
note: Puts real numbers on sbp-eia-it-2024, which recorded only the four headline changes. The 80 percent of equity ceiling and the similar-line-of-business condition are the two that bind most often in practice, and neither appears in any secondary coverage found.

claim: Para 13(II)(A2)(b) permits a Pakistani startup to incorporate a holding company abroad (the offshore flip) under general permission where the Pakistani operating company is a private limited or public unlisted company incorporated under the Companies Act 2017 for not more than 7 years and not formed by splitting up or reconstruction, has annual revenue below PKR 2 billion since incorporation, and has equity including retained earnings below PKR 300 million per its latest audited financials. The HoldCo must repatriate to Pakistan at least 80 percent of funds raised from abroad annually until USD 1 million, and thereafter at least 50 percent annually until USD 10 million cumulative, in each case net of dividends remitted by the OpCo. No remittance from Pakistan is allowed for the share transfer, and the OpCo must report share issuance to SBP within 30 days.
source: SBP FE Circular No. 01 of 2024, Annexure A, Para 13(II)(A2)(b)
note: Directly answers the Y Combinator / Delaware flip question for Pakistani startups, which is asked constantly and answered nowhere with the actual conditions. The three eligibility tests are cumulative and the 7-year and PKR 300 million equity limits exclude more companies than founders expect.

claim: FBR's own Overseas Pakistanis FAQ states the eligibility condition as: 'They are non-resident in Pakistan meaning their stay in a financial year in Pakistan is less than 183 days.' The FAQ makes no mention whatever of clause 82(d), the citizen limb, under which a Pakistani citizen who spends under 183 days in Pakistan can STILL be resident if he was not present in any other single country for more than 182 days or is not a resident taxpayer of any other country.
source: FBR Overseas Pakistanis FAQ, FAQs on filer rate under section 236C or 236K
note: STRONG material for Guide A. FBR's own public-facing guidance restates the popular oversimplification that residency is only about days in Pakistan. The guide can make the point without accusing anyone: even FBR's FAQ describes only the (a) test, so a reader who relies on it will miss the limb most likely to catch a perpetual traveller. Note also this FAQ describes 'financial year', where s.82 says 'tax year'.

claim: The FBR Overseas Pakistanis FAQ on s.236C/236K filer rates is of stale vintage as of September 2026. It presents banded rate tables 'after the amendments made through Finance Act, 2025' (236K at 1.5/2/2.5 percent by value band, 236C at 4.5/5/5.5 percent) and retains a 'Late filer' column. The Finance Act 2026 replaced these with a single flat s.236C rate of 2.75 percent and abolished the Late Filer category by omitting rule 1A of the Tenth Schedule.
source: FBR Overseas Pakistanis FAQ compared with Finance Act 2026
note: Another live instance of the project's documented failure mode: a genuinely official FBR page serving superseded figures. The PROCEDURE it describes is still useful and was already recorded under overseas-psid-filer-rate; the RATES on the same page are not. Cite the procedure, never the rate table.

claim: FBR prescribes no specific document to prove non-residence in the s.236C/236K overseas route. Its FAQ says the applicant declares 'his status as resident or non-resident and can upload documents in support thereof', and the Commissioner 'shall verify the documents attached, approve after verification'. No document type is named, no form number is given, and no tax residency certificate is required by the text.
source: FBR Overseas Pakistanis FAQ, procedure steps
note: Directly relevant to the s.82(d) proof question. The nearest thing to a published FBR procedure touching proof of non-residence leaves the evidence open and the decision to a Commissioner's discretion. This supports publishing the proof question as genuinely unresolved rather than inventing a checklist.

claim: The expression 'normal banking channels' is used at least nine times across the Income Tax Ordinance but is never defined in s.2 or anywhere else. The only interpretive text is the Explanation to s.111(4) inserted by the Finance Act 2022, which deems remittance through money service bureaus, exchange companies or money transfer operators to constitute foreign exchange remitted through normal banking channels 'as provided under this sub-section'.
source: Income Tax Ordinance consolidated to 30 June 2026
note: Two publishable points. First, the Explanation is expressly scoped to s.111(4) by the words 'under this sub-section', so it does not automatically carry to the other provisions using the same phrase, for example the sixty-day certificate in s.227C. Second, there is no general definition, which is an honest open question.

claim: s.116A(1) verbatim: 'Every resident taxpayer being an individual having foreign income of not less than ten thousand United States dollars or having foreign assets with a value of not less than one hundred thousand United States dollars shall furnish a statement, hereinafter referred to as the foreign income and assets statement, in the prescribed form and verified in the prescribed manner'. The obligation is confined to a RESIDENT taxpayer.
source: Income Tax Ordinance consolidated to 30 June 2026, s.116A(1)
note: Confirms the caller's thresholds verbatim from the post-FA2026 consolidation and adds the load-bearing qualifier: the duty attaches only to residents. This is the interlock between Guide A and Guide B. Residency decided under s.82 is what switches on s.116A, and with it the s.182 penalty of 2 percent of foreign income or asset value per year of default and the s.195A imprisonment exposure already recorded.

claim: FBR Circular No. 15 of 2022-23 (Income Tax and CVT), dated 21 July 2022, is FBR's explanatory circular on the Finance Act 2022. Its ENTIRE treatment of clause 82(d), under the heading 'Definition of Resident Individual', reads: 'The scope of the definition of resident individual has been further expanded through insertion of clause (d) to section 82. Now a person being a citizen of Pakistan whose stay in any other country is not more than one hundred and eighty-two days during a tax year or who is not a resident taxpayer of any other country will also be treated as resident individual for the purpose of the Ordinance.'
source: FBR Circular No. 15 of 2022-23, C.No.4(21) IT-Budget/2022, page 9
note: ANSWERS the question of what FBR has actually said about clause (d). It is four lines, and they only paraphrase the statute. FBR does NOT say what proves you are a resident taxpayer elsewhere, does not mention tax residency certificates, does not address treaty tie-breakers, and does not address the zero-tax-country case. Anything a consultant blog asserts on those points is not coming from this circular. Document verified as correct by its own header before use.

claim: The same FBR Circular No. 15 of 2022-23 explains the OTHER Explanation the Finance Act 2022 inserted into s.111, the one dispensing with a separate concealment notice where s.122(9) has been used. It says nothing at all about the Explanation inserted into s.111(4) deeming remittances through money service bureaus, exchange companies and money transfer operators to be through normal banking channels.
source: FBR Circular No. 15 of 2022-23, section on section 111
note: A clean negative finding. The s.111(4) Explanation is in the statute and is good law, but FBR has published no explanation of its scope, so questions such as whether a Wise or Remitly transfer qualifies, and what the encashment certificate must show, have no FBR guidance behind them. Publish as an open question.

claim: Section 82(ab), which made an individual resident if present in Pakistan for 120 days or more in the tax year AND 365 days or more across the four preceding years, was inserted by the Finance Act 2019 and OMITTED by the Finance Act 2021. It is not current law. A separate earlier clause (b), a 90-day plus 365-day test, was omitted by the Finance Act 2003.
source: Income Tax Ordinance 2001 consolidated to 30 June 2026, s.82 footnotes 4, 5 and 6
note: The 120-day rule is still widely cited by Pakistani tax blogs and diaspora forums as live law, and it is not. It survived only two tax years. This is a clean, checkable correction of the kind METHOD.md section 8 calls for: lead with it.

claim: The Income Tax Ordinance 2001 contains no provision governing how days of presence in Pakistan are counted for section 82: no rule on part-days, on days of arrival and departure, or on days in transit. Sections 81 to 84 set the residency tests and are silent on computation.
source: Income Tax Ordinance 2001 consolidated to 30 June 2026, ss.81-84, searched for computation provisions
note: NEGATIVE FINDING, and publish it as an open question rather than adopting a competitor's assertion. Several sources state confidently that a part-day counts as a full day; that rule is not in the Ordinance in the text read. It may exist in the Income Tax Rules 2002, which were NOT fetched, so the honest statement is that the Ordinance does not address it and a reader near the threshold should not rely on a blog's arithmetic. Do not assert either way.

claim: FBR's own live web page at fbr.gov.pk/section-82/152702, fetched 10 September 2026, prints an OBSOLETE version of section 82. It shows clause (ab), the 120-day plus 365-days-in-four-preceding-years test, which the Finance Act 2021 OMITTED, and it omits clause (d), the citizen limb which the Finance Act 2022 INSERTED. The page is therefore wrong in both directions at once: it states a test that no longer exists and hides the test most likely to catch an overseas Pakistani.
source: FBR section 82 page compared against Income Tax Ordinance consolidated to 30 June 2026
note: THE SINGLE MOST VALUABLE ITEM FOR GUIDE A, and a textbook case of this project's documented failure mode: a genuinely official source at the top of search results, five years out of date. It also explains WHY competitors get s.82 wrong, since this is the page a writer searching 'FBR section 82' lands on first. The correction is checkable by any reader in thirty seconds: open the FBR page, then open the consolidated Ordinance at s.82 and read footnote 5, which records the omission of clause (ab) by the Finance Act 2021. Pairs with the existing DEAD-ENDS note that fbr.gov.pk/section-<N>/<id> paths are unreliable; here the id does resolve to s.82, but the CONTENT is stale.

claim: A domestic disregarded entity wholly owned by one foreign person is treated as a corporation for section 6038A purposes and must file Form 5472 attached to a pro forma Form 1120. Only the name and address of the DE and items B and E on page 1 of the 1120 need be completed.
source: Instructions for Form 5472 (Rev. December 2024), 'Foreign-owned U.S. DE' and 'When and Where To File'; Treas. Reg. 301.7701-2(c)(2)(vi)
note: Applies to tax years of entities beginning after 31 Dec 2016 and ending on or after 13 Dec 2017 per 301.7701-2(e)(9). VINTAGE: instructions are Rev. 12-2024, used with the Dec 2023 revision of the form; this is the current revision on IRS.gov as at 10 Sep 2026.

claim: A foreign-owned U.S. DE cannot file Form 5472 electronically. It must fax the pro forma Form 1120 with Form 5472 attached to 855-887-7737, or mail it to Internal Revenue Service, 1973 Rulon White Blvd, M/S 6112 Attn: PIN Unit, Ogden, UT 84201, writing 'Foreign-owned U.S. DE' across the top of the Form 1120. These filers must NOT use the regular Form 1120 addresses.
source: Instructions for Form 5472 (Rev. 12-2024), 'Electronic Filing of Form 5472' and 'Dedicated mailing address'
note: The practical trap. The instructions carry an explicit CAUTION that the DE cannot e-file and must not use the standard 1120 address. Same rule applies to Form 7004 for an extension, which must go to the same fax/address with the Form 1120 code entered.

claim: The penalty for failure to file Form 5472 is USD 25,000, assessed for each taxable year with respect to which the failure occurs. If the failure continues more than 90 days after IRS notification, an additional USD 25,000 applies per related party for each 30-day period thereafter. There is no maximum. A substantially incomplete Form 5472 counts as a failure to file.
source: Treas. Reg. 1.6038A-4(a)(1) and (d); Instructions for Form 5472 (Rev. 12-2024) 'Penalties'; IRS International information reporting penalties page (updated 20 Aug 2026)
note: NOT inflation-adjusted. The regulation text reads '$25,000 shall be assessed for each taxable year'. Checked the IRS penalties page (20 Aug 2026), the 12-2024 instructions and eCFR 1.6038A-4: all state 25,000 flat. Reasonable cause defence exists under 1.6038A-4(b) with an affirmative showing under penalties of perjury.

claim: A foreign-owned U.S. DE with no trading income still files if it had any Part V transaction. Reg. 1.6038A-2(b)(3)(xi) makes 'any other transaction as defined by 1.482-1(i)(7), such as amounts paid or received in connection with the formation, dissolution, acquisition and disposition of the entity, including contributions to and distributions from the entity' a reportable transaction for a DE.
source: Treas. Reg. 1.6038A-2(b)(3)(xi), read via eCFR; Instructions for Form 5472 (Rev. 12-2024) Part V
note: Kills the 'my LLC was dormant so I do not file' assumption. Funding the LLC bank account or paying the registered agent from owner funds is itself a reportable transaction. The filing exception in the instructions requires NO Part IV, Part V AND Part VI transactions.

claim: Personal service income is sourced where the services are performed, regardless of where the contract was made, the place of payment, or the residence of the payer. IRS: 'The place, where the personal services are performed, generally determines the source of the personal service income, regardless of where the contract was made, or the place of payment, or the residence of the payer.'
source: IRS, Source of income - Personal service income (updated 06 Feb 2026); IRC 861(a)(3)/862(a)(3); Pub 519 (2025) Table 2-1
note: The load-bearing rule for section B of the US LLC guide. A Pakistani developer working from Lahore for a US client performs the services in Pakistan, so the fee is foreign-source under US law even though the payer and the LLC are American. Pub 519 Table 2-1 lists 'Personal services: Where services performed'.

claim: A US-Pakistan income tax convention exists and is in force: signed at Washington 1 July 1957, instruments of ratification exchanged at Karachi 21 May 1959. It is listed on IRS Table 3 as in effect and by FBR as 'In Force'. It has never been amended by protocol and is not modified by the MLI (the US is not an MLI party).
source: IRS Table 3 List of Tax Treaties (updated through 26 Sep 2025); IRS-hosted treaty text; FBR treaty summary
note: NOTE the URL: irs.gov/pub/irs-trty/pakistan.pdf is a 404. Effective-date discrepancy: treaty cover page and FBR say 1 Jan 1959, IRS Table 3 says 1 Jan 1960. Article XIX ties effect to the year ratifications were exchanged (1959). Immaterial to any live position but do not state one date as though sources agree.

claim: Article III(2) of the 1957 US-Pakistan convention is a force-of-attraction rule: 'A Pakistan enterprise shall not be subject to United States tax in respect of its industrial or commercial profits unless it is engaged in trade or business in the United States through a permanent establishment situated therein. If it is so engaged, United States tax may be imposed upon the entire income of such enterprise from sources within the United States.'
source: US-Pakistan Income Tax Convention 1957, Article III(2), quoted verbatim from the IRS-hosted text
note: Verified verbatim against the PDF text. Modern OECD treaties limit US tax to profits ATTRIBUTABLE to the PE; this 1957 treaty does not. Once a PE exists the US may tax the enterprise's entire US-source income. Separately, Article II(1)(l) EXCLUDES 'remuneration for labor or personal services' from 'industrial or commercial profits', so Article III does not shelter freelance service fees at all.

claim: Article XI(2) exempts a Pakistani resident from US tax on personal (including professional) services performed within the US only if ALL THREE of: (a) present in the US on a temporary visit not exceeding 183 days in aggregate in the year, (b) the services are performed for or on behalf of a resident of Pakistan, and (c) the profits or remuneration are subject to Pakistan tax.
source: US-Pakistan Income Tax Convention 1957, Article XI(2), quoted verbatim; IRS Pub 901 (Rev. September 2024)
note: The conditions are conjunctive. Condition (b) disqualifies the typical case: a Pakistani freelancer billing a US client is not performing services for or on behalf of a PAKISTANI resident, so the 183-day count alone does not help. Widely misread as a simple day-count test.

claim: FinCEN's final rule of 11 August 2026, effective 14 August 2026, permanently removes the BOI reporting requirement for US companies and US persons. 'Reporting companies' now means ONLY entities formed under the law of a foreign country that have registered to do business in a US State or Tribal jurisdiction. A US-formed LLC therefore has no FinCEN BOI obligation regardless of its owners' nationality.
source: FinCEN Final Rule: Questions and Answers (Aug 2026) Q1 and Q3; FinCEN news release 11 Aug 2026; FinCEN BOI landing page
note: VINTAGE CRITICAL. This SUPERSEDES the 26 March 2025 interim final rule, which most published content still describes, and both supersede the original CTA position. The test is PLACE OF FORMATION, not owner nationality: a Wyoming LLC owned wholly by Pakistani residents is a US-formed entity and is exempt. Q3 is the operative sentence.

claim: A newly issued EIN can fail Stripe's tax ID verification because IRS records lag. Stripe: 'On average, this takes the IRS 3-4 weeks.' Stripe accepts an uploaded SS-4 confirmation letter as the workaround for TINs issued within the last ~3 months. IRS states an EIN can be used immediately to open a bank account or file a paper return, but to 'Wait up to 2 weeks to: Pass an IRS Taxpayer ID Number (TIN) Matching Program, E-file a tax return, Make tax deposits and pay electronically.'
source: Stripe Support, 'What to do if your newly-issued US tax ID number (TIN) is not verifying'; IRS Employer ID Numbers page (updated 17 Jul 2026)
note: UPGRADES finding stripe-ein-lag from unverified/tier 3. Both halves now come from the primary parties. Note the two figures differ and should be quoted separately, not merged: Stripe says 3-4 weeks for its own IRS check, IRS says up to 2 weeks for TIN Matching. The mechanism is IRS TIN Matching, which the IRS page names explicitly. Do NOT state the '2-3 weeks' figure from the original vendor claim: neither primary source says that.

claim: A foreign responsible party without an SSN or ITIN can still obtain an EIN: 'Enter “foreign” or N/A on line 7b if the responsible party doesn't have and is ineligible to obtain an SSN or ITIN. An entry is required.' The online EIN application is available only to applicants with a US legal residence or principal place of business, and requires the principal officer to hold an SSN/EIN/ITIN. International applicants may apply by phone on 267-941-1099 (not toll free), 6:00 a.m. to 11:00 p.m. Eastern, Monday to Friday, or by fax to 304-707-9471 from outside the US, receiving the EIN generally within 4 business days.
source: Instructions for Form SS-4 (Rev. December 2025)
note: Answers the practical blocker for Pakistani founders. The online route is closed to them; phone is the fast route and is international-only. Vendor guides that promise 'EIN online in a day' are describing a route this audience cannot use.

claim: The 1 percent remittance transfer excise tax under IRC 4475, effective for transfers after 31 December 2025, applies ONLY where the sender provides cash, a money order, a cashier's check or other similar physical instrument. Transfers funded from an account at a financial institution or by US-issued debit or credit card are outside the charge.
source: IRC 4475; IRS news release on proposed regulations, 10 April 2026
note: Relevant because it is being mis-described to Pakistani audiences as a tax on all remittances. A Stripe payout or bank wire from a US LLC to Pakistan is NOT within IRC 4475. Worth an explicit correction.

claim: A Delaware LLC pays an annual tax of USD 400, due on or before 1 June, with no annual report requirement. Delaware Division of Corporations: 'All Domestic and Foreign Limited Liability Companies, Limited Partnerships, and General Partnerships formed or registered in Delaware are required to pay an annual tax of $400.00. There is no requirement to file an Annual Report.' Failure to pay incurs a penalty of USD 200 plus 1.5 percent interest per month on tax and penalty. There is no proration.
source: Delaware Division of Corporations, LLC/LP/GP Franchise Tax Instructions; Delaware HB 400 (signed 21 May 2026)
note: CORRECTION TARGET. HB 400 raised the LLC annual tax from 300 to 400. Delaware's own page now states 400, so it is the operative figure. Practically every vendor guide still prints 300. Also note vendors routinely conflate the LLC rule with the CORPORATION rule (annual report plus franchise tax, minimum 175, due 1 March): Delaware LLCs file no annual report at all.

claim: s.101(2) Income Tax Ordinance 2001: 'Business income of a resident person shall be Pakistan-source income to the extent to which the income is derived from any business carried on in Pakistan.' s.11(5): the income of a resident person is computed taking into account both Pakistan-source and foreign-source amounts.
source: Income Tax Ordinance 2001 consolidated to 30 June 2026, ss.101(2) and 11(5)
note: Important qualifier for the US LLC guide. Where the owner runs the LLC from Pakistan, the profit may be PAKISTAN-source business income under s.101(2), not foreign-source. That affects the framing: the LLC is a declarable foreign ASSET under s.116A, but its profit is not automatically 'foreign income'. Do not assert a single characterisation without stating the s.101(2) test.

claim: s.103(1): a resident taxpayer deriving foreign-source income on which foreign income tax has been PAID is allowed a credit equal to the lesser of the foreign income tax paid or the Pakistan tax payable on that income.
source: Income Tax Ordinance 2001 consolidated to 30 June 2026, s.103(1)
note: The structural point competitors miss when they invoke the treaty: if the US LLC lawfully pays ZERO US federal income tax, there is no foreign tax paid, so there is no s.103 credit and nothing for the treaty to relieve. The Pakistani liability is the whole liability. 'The treaty prevents double taxation' is therefore a non-answer for this fact pattern.

claim: Syed Shabbar Zaidi, a former Chairman of the FBR, published an opinion in Business Recorder arguing that s.82(d) is bad law. His central point: 'The Finance Act, 2022 has virtually decided that a Pakistani citizen can be taxed in Pakistan even if he never comes to Pakistan.' He gives worked examples: a citizen staying 160 days in Pakistan and 100 and 105 days in States A and B is deemed a Pakistani tax resident; so is one staying 100, 100 and 165 days in States A, B and C where every state treats him as non-resident on its own 183-day test. He calls clause (d) 'effectively extraterritorial', says its validity 'is required to be examined in that perspective', and observes that in practical terms the limb 'is not implementable as staying in another country for certain days, falls outside Pakistan's regulatory system'.
source: Syed Shabbar Zaidi, 'Determining an individual's residency status: some taxation anomalies', Business Recorder, mirrored at Riphah International University information portal
note: High-authority tier 3: the author is a former FBR Chairman and was the official who introduced the 2019 amendment he discusses. Original at brecorder.com/news/40193434 returns a hard 403 to curl even with a browser UA and same-site Referer; the Riphah mirror carries the full text including the author credit, and needs -k because the certificate chain does not verify. Attribute to Zaidi as informed criticism, never as a statement of what the law is. His worked examples are the clearest illustration available of how clause (d) catches a genuine perpetual traveller.

claim: Zaidi argues s.82(d) was copied from India's section 6(1A), inserted in 2020, but copied incorrectly. India's provision applies only to a citizen with Indian-source-excluded total income above fifteen lakh rupees who is not liable to tax anywhere by reason of domicile or residence, and it feeds India's 'resident but not ordinarily resident' status, under which foreign income is taxed only if derived from a business controlled in or a profession set up in India. Pakistan has no 'resident but not ordinarily resident' concept, so a person caught by s.82(d) becomes a full resident taxable on worldwide income under s.11(5), with no income threshold and no requirement that the foreign income have any connection to Pakistan.
source: Zaidi, Business Recorder opinion, mirrored at Riphah information portal
note: The comparison is checkable against the Indian statute and against the Ordinance, where the absence of a 'not ordinarily resident' concept is verifiable by its absence. Strong material for an open-questions section: it explains WHY clause (d) bites harder in Pakistan than its Indian model does. Treat the Indian text as Zaidi's quotation, not as independently verified by us.

claim: Zaidi states: 'The dates of arrival and departure are included as to be in Pakistan for the purposes of stay in Pakistan. Such dates are reflected in the entry or exit stamps made on immigration counters established by the Government of Pakistan.'
source: Zaidi, Business Recorder opinion, mirrored at Riphah information portal
note: DO NOT PUBLISH AS LAW. This is the only substantive statement found anywhere on how days are counted, and it has no statutory basis: the Ordinance contains no part-day, arrival or departure rule at all. Publish as the settled practice a former FBR Chairman describes, expressly flagged as practice rather than statute, alongside the finding that the statute is silent. The honest framing is that both endpoints counting is the conventional reading and the safe assumption, but a taxpayer near the boundary cannot point to a provision. | SUPERSEDED by rule14-day-counting-verbatim. RESOLVED, and it upgrades this from practitioner statement to law. Rule 14 of the Income Tax RULES 2002 says exactly this: a part-day counts as a whole day including the day of arrival and the day of departure. We had searched only the Ordinance and wrongly concluded nothing prescribed it.

claim: PwC Worldwide Tax Summaries, last reviewed 24 August 2026, states the Pakistan individual residence tests as presence in Pakistan of 183 days or more in a tax year (1 July to 30 June), and includes the citizen limb: 'a person is a citizen of Pakistan and is not present in any other country for more than 182 days during the tax year or who is not a resident taxpayer of any other country.' It makes no mention of a 120-day test.
source: PwC Worldwide Tax Summaries, Pakistan, Individual, Residence
note: Independent tier 2 corroboration of both limbs and of the 183/182 asymmetry, with a review date after the Finance Act 2026. Its silence on the 120-day test corroborates that clause (ab) is gone, which is exactly what FBR's own s.82 page gets wrong.

claim: The 1957 US-Pakistan convention contains NO limitation on benefits article, no 'beneficial owner' concept, no services PE, no fees-for-technical-services article, no capital gains article, no modern mutual agreement or exchange of information article, and no arbitration. IRS Table 1 shows Pakistan interest at 30 percent (no treaty reduction), dividends 30/15 percent, royalties 0 percent.
source: US-Pakistan Income Tax Convention 1957 full text, keyword-searched; IRS Table 1 Tax Rates on Income Other Than Personal Service Income
note: Predates the 1963 OECD Draft Model. A reader who assumes the modern 15/5/10 withholding pattern will be wrong: there is NO interest rate reduction at all. Also not modified by the MLI, since the US is not an MLI party, so no principal purpose test applies. URL confirmed 200 on 10 Sep 2026; note that the treaty TABLES live under /pub/irs-lbi/ while the treaty TEXTS live under /pub/irs-trty/.

claim: 'Pakistan has a Double Taxation Avoidance Agreement (DTAA) with the United States. This prevents double taxation on the same income.' as an answer to whether a Pakistani-owned US LLC is taxed twice
source: vendor formation sites (wyomingllc.co and others)
note: REJECTED AS AN ANSWER, though a treaty does exist. Three defects. (1) It is a 1957 convention with a force-of-attraction PE rule and no LOB, not a modern DTAA. (2) Article II(1)(l) excludes remuneration for personal services from 'industrial or commercial profits', so the business profits article does not cover freelance fees. (3) Structurally it is a non-answer: where the LLC lawfully pays zero US tax there is no double taxation to relieve and no s.103 credit, because s.103 requires foreign tax PAID. Cite the treaty for what it does, never as reassurance.

claim: Section 111(4) originally contained no monetary cap: as substituted by the Finance Act 2004 it read simply that sub-section (1) does not apply to any amount of foreign exchange remitted from outside Pakistan through normal banking channels encashed into rupees by a scheduled bank with a certificate produced. The five million rupee per tax year ceiling was introduced later and appears in the sub-section as substituted by the Finance Act 2021, and the current text carries it.
source: Income Tax Ordinance 2001 consolidated to 30 June 2026, s.111(4) and footnotes 4 and 5
note: EXPLAINS why so many sources describe s.111(4) as an unlimited shield: for roughly seventeen years it was one. Those pages are not inventing the position, they are describing repealed law and have not been updated. This is the cleanest correction available on the remittance guide and it is checkable from the footnotes.

claim: waystax.com states: 'Inward foreign remittance received through official banking channels is exempt from income tax up to the equivalent of USD 100,000 per year' and 'Source disclosure required? No, for amounts within the limit'. This is wrong twice over. The s.111(4) threshold is Rs 5 million in a tax year, not USD 100,000, and s.111(4) confers no exemption from income tax at all: it disapplies s.111(1) only.
source: waystax.com remittance filing page, fetched 10 September 2026
note: CHECKABLE CORRECTION for Guide B, and the likely mechanism of the error is worth naming: USD 100,000 is the FOREIGN ASSETS threshold in s.116A, a different section serving a different purpose. The figure has been transplanted onto s.111(4) and converted from a filing trigger into an exemption ceiling. Naming the mechanism is more useful to a reader than simply calling the number wrong.

claim: kambohassociates.com states 'Money sent by an overseas family member (parent, sibling, spouse, child) to support Pakistan-resident family members is not taxable income in Pakistan' and 'Family support remittances are completely tax-exempt in Pakistan if received through banking channels', with no monetary cap mentioned anywhere and no Finance Act or tax year cited.
source: kambohassociates.com foreign remittance page, fetched 10 September 2026
note: The uncapped framing matches the PRE-Finance-Act-2021 text of s.111(4) exactly, which supports the finding that these restatements are stale rather than fabricated. Note the conclusion that a genuine family maintenance gift is not income can be right for its own reason, since a gift is not income under a head of income in s.11, but that reasoning is not s.111(4) and the page does not offer it.

claim: As of 2026 the Rs 5 million s.111(4) threshold remains in force and is publicly reported as under government review, not changed. Press reporting describes the government considering either removing the Rs 5 million limit entirely or raising it, on the view that it has been eroded by inflation and rupee depreciation.
source: Express Tribune reporting on proposals to amend s.111(4)
note: Corroborates from a second direction that the cap is live: the fact that removing it requires amending s.111(4) is itself confirmation the cap sits there now. Useful for a 'what may change' note, but the guide must state clearly that as at the Finance Act 2026 nothing has changed. Treat all figures in the press coverage as reporting of proposals, never as law.

claim: Syed Shabbar Zaidi identifies a second, separate statutory regime sitting alongside s.111(4): 'Section 5 of the Foreign Currency Accounts (Protection) Ordinance, 2001 inter alia overrides the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001.' He describes private foreign currency accounts, maintainable by individuals, which can be fed either by purchase of foreign currency from money changers or by receipt of funds from abroad, and argues the conjunctive operation of that regime with s.111(4) should be delinked.
source: Syed Shabbar Zaidi, 'Private foreign currency account and Section 111(4): the revolving circle', Business Recorder, mirrored at Riphah information portal
note: FLAGGED FOR FOLLOW-UP, do not publish the override claim until the Foreign Currency Accounts (Protection) Ordinance 2001 s.5 is read directly. If it holds it matters for Guide B, because it means s.111(4) is not the only protection in play and a foreign currency account has its own statutory shield. Also note this article PREDATES the Finance Act 2021 cap: it describes the s.111(4) immunity as unlimited throughout, which is further evidence that the 'unlimited' framing circulating online is stale rather than invented.

claim: Treas. Reg. 1.864-2(a): 'engaged in trade or business within the United States' includes the performance of personal services within the United States at any time within the taxable year, subject to a de minimis exception in 1.864-2(b) for a nonresident alien temporarily present not more than 90 days whose compensation does not exceed USD 3,000 in aggregate. IRS states foreign persons are generally engaged in a US trade or business when personal services are performed in the US, and that the activities must be considerable, continuous and regular.
source: Treas. Reg. 1.864-2(a) and (b); IRS Effectively Connected Income (ECI) page, updated 18 Aug 2026; Pub 519 (2025)
note: The statutory trigger is services performed WITHIN the United States. Pub 519 (2025): 'You are usually engaged in a U.S. trade or business when you perform personal services in the United States.' Combined with the s.861(a)(3) sourcing rule, work done from Pakistan is foreign-source and outside the ETBUS trigger on its face.

claim: Whether a Pakistani-resident owner of a US LLC performing all work from Pakistan has ECI is fact-dependent, not a clean statutory no. Pub 519 also states: 'If you own and operate a business in the United States selling services, products, or merchandise, you are, with certain exceptions, engaged in a trade or business in the United States.'
source: IRS Pub 519 (2025), 'Business operations'; Treas. Reg. 1.864-2; IRC 864(b)
note: FLAG UNCERTAINTY RATHER THAN GIVING A CLEAN ANSWER. Two IRS formulations sit in tension: the services test looks to WHERE SERVICES ARE PERFORMED (favouring no ECI for remote Pakistani work), while the 'own and operate a business in the United States' formulation is about the business's location. Neither IRS page resolves the case of a US-formed LLC whose only human activity happens abroad. Risk factors that can flip it: US-based employees, contractors or a dependent agent acting for the LLC; a US office or fixed place of business; inventory or fulfilment in the US; owner travel performing work while physically in the US. No IRS page, revenue ruling or regulation located that squarely addresses the remote-owner US LLC fact pattern. Do NOT publish 'a Wyoming LLC owned by a Pakistani pays zero US tax' as an unqualified rule.

claim: Pub 519: a nonresident alien individual engaged or considered to be engaged in a trade or business in the United States must file Form 1040-NR, and 'You must file even if: a. Your income did not come from a trade or business conducted in the United States, b. You have no income from U.S. sources, or c. Your income is exempt from income tax.'
source: IRS Publication 519 (2025), 'Nonresident Aliens' under What, When, and Where To File
note: The consequence of the ETBUS question that competitors omit entirely. If the owner IS engaged in a US trade or business, the personal 1040-NR duty arises even with zero US-source income and zero tax. The Form 5472 duty sits on the LLC and is separate from this.

claim: Under Para 13(II)(A1), Chapter 20 FE Manual, an IT-sector company has THREE funding routes for equity investment abroad, all under Authorized Dealer general permission (no prior SBP approval): (a) unlimited to the extent of funds in its Exporters' Special Foreign Currency Account, no bank designation needed; (b) unlimited to the extent of funds in a Special Foreign Currency Account holding equity raised from abroad, no designation needed; (c) for IT companies not yet exporting or without sufficient ESFCA/SFCA balance, the higher of average net profit of the last three financial years or USD 100,000, and this route DOES require prior designation of an Authorized Dealer under Para 13(IV).
source: SBP FE Manual Chapter 20 Para 13(II)(A1)(2), consolidated 11 Sep 2025; identical text in FE Circular 01 of 11 July 2024 Annexure-A
note: The USD 100,000 / average-net-profit cap applies ONLY to route (c). Routes (a) and (b) are capped by the account balance, not by a stated figure. Consultant blogs that quote 'USD 100,000' as the general IT limit are describing only the fallback route.

claim: Para 13(II)(A1)(3)(i) caps total investment abroad at 80% of the applicant's equity at any point in time (adjusted for investments in subsidiaries/associates, goodwill, deferred tax assets and receivables from related entities) for a non-listed company, or 80% of enterprise value for a listed company. This is an overarching ceiling that applies to all three A1 funding routes.
source: SBP FE Manual Chapter 20 Para 13(II)(A1)(3)(i)

claim: Para 13(II)(D), Chapter 20 grants resident INDIVIDUALS general permission for only three things: (1) shares of LISTED companies abroad, max USD 25,000 per calendar year and max 1% of the investee company; (2) employee stock option plans of a foreign parent, max USD 50,000 per calendar year and max 3%; (3) sweat equity received without monetary consideration, max 20%. Establishing or acquiring a private company abroad (a US LLC, UK Ltd or UAE free zone company) is NOT within any Category D general permission. Categories A1, A2 and B are available only to companies.
source: SBP FE Manual Chapter 20 Para 13(II)(D), consolidated 11 Sep 2025
note: HIGH CONSEQUENCE. This is the freelancer/personal-US-LLC question. The permission is by category, and no category fits an individual incorporating a private foreign entity. The residual route is an exemption/waiver application to Exchange Policy Department under Para 13(IV)(3), which is discretionary, not a general permission. Do not state that an individual is flatly prohibited by name: state that no general permission covers it, so it needs specific SBP permission.

claim: Para 13(III), Chapter 20 imposes four post-investment duties on the investor: submit documentary evidence of the establishment/acquisition within one month through the Authorized Dealer; file a return to SBP on prescribed form V-100 within one month of making the investment; submit audited financials of the investee company annually; and repatriate dividends and disinvestment proceeds (including capital gains) through normal banking channels, converted to PKR, with the original Proceeds Realization Certificate filed with SBP. Separately the Authorized Dealer must report to SBP on Appendix V-150 within three working days of the transaction.
source: SBP FE Manual Chapter 20 Para 13(III) and Para 13(II)(A1)(3)(viii)
note: Form V-100 is the investor's return; Appendix V-150 is the bank's. Repatriated proceeds may NOT be credited to a foreign currency account.

claim: As of 10 September 2026 no SBP circular after FE Circular No. 01 of 11 July 2024 has amended Para 13 of Chapter 20 (Equity Investment Abroad). Established by reading the full SBP circular index back to February 2024 (270 entries, offsets P0 to P240) and by checking the footnotes of the FE Manual Chapter 20 consolidated on 11 September 2025, whose Para 13 carries footnote 22 citing 'FE Circular No. 01 dated July 11, 2024' as its authority and no later citation.
source: SBP circulars index and FE Manual Chapter 20 footnote 22
note: VINTAGE CHECK. Three post-2024 circulars touch nearby ground but NOT Para 13: F.E Circular 01 of 28 Aug 2025 (PESIA reporting system for EIA); FE Circular 02 of 25 May 2026 (Chapter 20 Para 7, inbound share registration); FE Circular 03 of 25 May 2026 (NSRS, inbound). Note the live Chapter 20 PDF is the Sep 2025 consolidation and therefore does NOT itself contain the May 2026 Para 7 amendment.

claim: F.E Circular No. 01 of 28 August 2025 implemented the Performance Evaluation System for Investment Abroad (PESIA), an online reporting mechanism requiring Authorized Dealers to report all Equity Investment Abroad transactions monthly through SBP's Data Acquisition Portal via ten Data File Structures. It also required retrospective reporting of legacy EIA data: Phase I covering transactions from 10 February 2021 to 31 July 2025 by 28 November 2025, and Phase II covering transactions before 9 February 2021 by 28 February 2026.
source: SBP F.E Circular No. 01 of 2025, 28 August 2025
note: Directly relevant to the 'I already set one up quietly' question: SBP has been building a retrospective dataset of equity investment abroad. The circular also warns of enforcement action against delinquent ADs under FERA 1947.

claim: Para 12(iv)(a), Chapter 12 of the FE Manual, as amended by EPD Circular Letter No. 06 of 6 April 2026, allows IT Companies and Freelancers to retain in their Exporters' Special Foreign Currency Accounts the HIGHER of USD 5,000 per month or 50% of export proceeds. Para 12(v)(c) expressly permits ESFCA funds to be used for capital and financial account transactions 'such as equity investment abroad', in line with Chapter 20. Para 12(i)(a) defines IT Companies to include sole proprietorships and partnership firms registered with PSEB or P@SHA.
source: SBP EPD Circular Letter No. 06 of 2026 Annexure-A, revised Para 12 Chapter 12
note: CURRENT VINTAGE for ESFCA, supersedes earlier retention percentages. Note the definitional tension: Chapter 12 counts a sole proprietorship as an 'IT Company' for ESFCA purposes, but Chapter 20 Para 13 grants the A1 investment-abroad permission to companies, with individuals confined to Category D.

claim: Section 23(1) of the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act 1947 makes contravention of the Act, or of any rule, direction or order made under it, punishable with rigorous imprisonment of up to five years, or a fine, or both, tried by a Tribunal under s.23A, and the Tribunal may additionally order confiscation of the security or property in respect of which the contravention took place. Section 23(2) makes the offence cognizable and non-bailable. Under s.23(3) a Tribunal cannot take cognizance except on a written complaint by a person authorised by SBP, and where the contravention is doing an act without permission, no complaint may be made unless the accused has first been given an opportunity to show that he had such permission.
source: Foreign Exchange Regulation Act 1947, ss.23, 23A
note: The s.23(3) proviso (opportunity to show permission) and the SBP-complaint gate are the practical brakes: SBP controls whether a prosecution starts. Also s.23B provides for adjudicating officers, an administrative penalty route short of the Tribunal.

claim: Section 5(1)(e) FERA 1947 provides that, save with SBP exemption, no person in or resident in Pakistan shall make any payment to or for the credit of any person as consideration for or in association with the acquisition by any person of property outside Pakistan. Section 13(1) separately restricts taking or sending any security out of Pakistan and transferring a security to a person resident outside Pakistan. Section 2(e) defines 'foreign security' as any security issued elsewhere than in Pakistan.
source: Foreign Exchange Regulation Act 1947, ss.2(e), 5(1)(e), 13(1)
note: s.5(1)(e) is the provision that bites on funding a foreign entity, and it is drafted around the PAYMENT, not around where the payer banks. But note the genuine carve-out in s.5(2)(b): the section does not render unlawful a payment made with foreign exchange received by way of salary or payment for services not arising from business in Pakistan. That clause is the strongest textual support for the 'I funded it from offshore earnings' position and it should be presented as an arguable reading, not as settled.

claim: No published SBP instrument provides an amnesty, condonation or retrospective-approval route for a foreign entity already established by a Pakistani resident without permission. The only mechanism in Chapter 20 is Para 13(IV)(3), under which an Authorized Dealer forwards an application for exemption or waiver from Para 13(II) A1, A2, B or D to the Director, Exchange Policy Department, with the bank's own review and specific recommendation; SBP will not entertain an application lacking that recommendation. This is prospective and discretionary and is not described anywhere as a regularisation route.
source: SBP FE Manual Chapter 20 Para 13(IV)(2)-(3); absence established by sweeping the SBP circular index Feb 2024 to Sep 2026
note: Publish as an OPEN QUESTION. The honest answer is that the published material does not address it. The 2018 Foreign Assets (Declaration and Repatriation) Act was a TAX amnesty, long expired, and did not cure FERA contraventions. Do not tell readers there is a clean fix; tell them to take it to their AD and to counsel.

claim: The Foreign Currency Accounts (Protection) Ordinance 2001 (Ordinance L of 2001, gazetted 28 September 2001) protects the RIGHT TO OPERATE a foreign currency account, not the source of the money in it. s.3: 'No person holding a foreign currency account shall be deprived of his right to hold or operate such account or in any manner be restricted temporarily or permanently to lawfully sell, withdraw, remit, transfer, use as security or take out foreign currency therefrom within or outside Pakistan.' s.5(1): 'Subject to subsection (2), the provisions of this Ordinance shall have effect notwithstanding anything contained in the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act, 1947, the Customs Act, 1969, the Income Tax Ordinance, 1979 (XXXI of 1979) or any other law for the time being in force.' s.5(2) provides only that the protection is in addition to, and not in derogation of, the Protection of Economic Reforms Act 1992. 'Foreign currency account' is defined in s.2(c) as an account opened with an authorised dealer AFTER 28 May 1998. Nothing in the Ordinance addresses the source of funds or confers any immunity from tax.
source: Foreign Currency Accounts (Protection) Ordinance 2001, full text
note: NARROWS the Zaidi claim recorded under fcap-ordinance-2001-s5-override, which should not be published as he framed it. Two points matter for Guide B. First, the override in s.5(1) names the Income Tax Ordinance 1979, which was repealed and replaced by the 2001 Ordinance; whether the reference carries forward is a live construction question we should not resolve ourselves, though s.5(1) also says 'or any other law for the time being in force'. Second, and more usefully, the protection is about not being deprived of the ACCOUNT. It is not a source-of-funds shield, so it does not do what s.111(4) does and does not extend s.111(4). Guide B can use this to close off a confusion rather than to open one. Text is from a law-site mirror, tier 1 by content but hosted secondary: confirm against the Pakistan Code PDF before quoting at length, as the Pakistan Code page is an index whose text sits behind a PDF link.

claim: 6 Del. C. s.18-1107(b) sets the Delaware LLC annual tax at USD 400 ('an annual tax, for the use of the State of Delaware, in the amount of $400'), and USD 100 per registered series. s.18-1107(c): due and payable on the first day of June following the close of the calendar year; unpaid tax bears interest at 1.5 percent for each month or portion thereof until fully paid. s.18-1107(e) adds a USD 200 penalty. There is no annual report for a Delaware LLC.
source: 6 Del. C. s.18-1107(b),(c),(e); Delaware Division of Corporations LLC/LP/GP Franchise Tax Instructions
note: VINTAGE TRAP, and a textbook METHOD.md case: corp.delaware.gov serves BOTH figures. The Alt Entity Tax Instructions page says 400; the Tax FAQ page and revenue.delaware.gov still say 300. The STATUTE settles it at 400, quoted verbatim and confirmed independently by two routes. HB 400, signed 21 May 2026, made the increase from 300. Any source saying 300 is stale. Also: do not conflate with the Delaware CORPORATION regime (annual report plus franchise tax, minimum 175, due 1 March), which is what several vendor guides describe.

claim: W.S. 17-29-209(a): the Wyoming LLC annual report license tax is USD 60 or USD .0002 per dollar of capital, property and assets located and employed in Wyoming, whichever is greater, due on the first day of the anniversary month of organization. The initial Articles of Organization filing fee is USD 100.
source: Wyoming LLC Act W.S. 17-29-209(a); Wyoming SOS fee schedule effective 1 July 2026; SOS tax worksheet rules
note: FETCH CAVEAT: all .wyo.gov hosts were unreachable at TCP level from this environment (connection timeout, NOT a 403, so the UA+Referer retry could not apply). Figures were recovered from Wayback captures of the state's OWN PDFs (May-Aug 2026, documents self-dated 'Revised June 2026' and 'Schedule Effective July 1st, 2026'). Official documents, archived rather than live. RE-CONFIRM against a live sos.wyo.gov fetch before publishing. Because the tax is based on assets LOCATED AND EMPLOYED IN WYOMING, a Pakistani-owned LLC with no Wyoming assets pays the USD 60 minimum; break-even is USD 300,000 of Wyoming assets.

claim: A New Mexico LLC files NO annual report. The New Mexico LLC Act (NMSA Ch. 53 Art. 19, ss.53-19-1 to 53-19-74) contains no annual report provision, in contrast to the corporation article (biennial) and 54-1A-1003 for LLPs (annual). Initial filing fee is USD 50 under NMSA 53-19-63(A).
source: NMSA Chapter 53 Article 19 full statute text, searched across all 74 sections
note: Confirmed as a NEGATIVE by reading the complete Act rather than by absence of search results, which is the only sound way to establish it. TRAP: a widely circulating '$10 annual report, $10 late penalty, $25 reinstatement' for NM LLCs is CORPORATION data and does not apply to LLCs. NM SOS web pages are JavaScript-rendered and yielded no extractable fee text, so these come from the statute rather than a current SOS fee schedule.

claim: In none of Wyoming, New Mexico or Delaware can an owner living outside the US serve as their own registered agent. Wyoming: the SOS Articles of Organization form states 'The registered agent must have a physical address in Wyoming. A Drop Box is not acceptable. A PO Box is acceptable if listed in addition to a physical address.' New Mexico: NMSA 53-19-5(A)(2) requires an individual resident of New Mexico or an entity with a place of business in NM at the registered office. Delaware: 6 Del. C. s.18-104 requires a registered office in Delaware whose address 'shall include the street, number, city and postal code'.
source: Wyoming SOS LLC Articles of Organization form; NMSA 53-19-5(A); 6 Del. C. s.18-104
note: All three therefore require a commercial registered agent for a Pakistan-based founder, which is a recurring annual cost vendors fold into 'formation' pricing. The RA address becomes public record in each state. Wyoming's physical-address quote comes from the SOS FORM, not the statute text, which was not fetched.

claim: New Mexico gross receipts tax reaches 'performing services in New Mexico, and performing services outside of New Mexico, the product of which is initially used in New Mexico'. Businesses without a physical presence are subject to GRT if they have at least USD 100,000 of taxable gross receipts in the previous calendar year.
source: New Mexico Taxation and Revenue Department, Gross receipts overview
note: The reason New Mexico is not simply 'the cheapest state'. GRT applies to SERVICES, not only goods, which is the relevant category for this audience. That said the charge keys on services performed IN New Mexico or first used there, so a Pakistan-based owner serving non-NM clients is generally outside it. The specific rate RANGE (often quoted 5.125-8.6875 percent) was NOT verified from a readable official page: do not publish a rate.

claim: Wyoming has no state income tax
source: widely repeated, no official page fetched
note: NOT CONFIRMED FROM AN OFFICIAL SOURCE in this pass: revenue.wyo.gov was unreachable alongside the other .wyo.gov hosts. Almost certainly true and universally reported, but per the research store's own rule it is not citable until a live revenue.wyo.gov or statute fetch confirms it. Do not publish as sourced. Same status for the Wyoming late penalty: no dollar penalty for a late LLC annual report was found; the consequence is administrative dissolution, and the commonly cited USD 50 late fee and '60 days' window could NOT be verified in W.S. 17-29-701.

claim: s.51(2) verbatim: 'Where a citizen of Pakistan leaves Pakistan during a tax year and remains abroad during that tax year, any income chargeable under the head Salary earned by him outside Pakistan during that year shall be exempt from tax under this Ordinance.' This is a true exemption and it is NOT conditioned on the individual being non-resident.
source: Income Tax Ordinance consolidated to 30 June 2026, s.51(2), added by the Finance Act 2003
note: THE MOST IMPORTANT PRACTICAL FIND FOR GUIDE A, and it substantially softens the s.82(d) alarm that dominates existing coverage. A salaried Pakistani abroad who is dragged into residence by clause (d) is resident and so within s.11(5) worldwide scope, but his foreign SALARY is separately exempt under s.51(2) on its own terms. The relief turns on leaving Pakistan and remaining abroad, not on residency status. So for the large salaried segment of the diaspora, clause (d) has far less bite than the consultant commentary implies. Note the limits carefully: it covers salary only, so business profits, freelancing income, rent, dividends, interest and capital gains are NOT covered, and clause (d) still switches on s.116A reporting and s.114 filing. Guide A should present this as the correction that matters most to the ordinary reader, and be precise that it is an exemption for one head of income and not a general shelter.

claim: s.50: the foreign-source income of an individual who is a resident individual solely by reason of the individual's employment and who is present in Pakistan for a period or periods not exceeding three years is exempt from tax. By s.50(2) this does not apply to income from a business established in Pakistan, or to any foreign-source income brought into or received in Pakistan by the person.
source: Income Tax Ordinance consolidated to 30 June 2026, s.50
note: Relevant to the reverse flow, a foreign national or returning Pakistani posted INTO Pakistan. Note the sharp carve-out in s.50(2)(b): bringing the foreign income into Pakistan destroys the exemption, which is a genuine remittance trap and a good contrast for Guide B, since here the ROUTE of the money does change the tax outcome, unlike under s.111(4).

claim: s.51(1): any foreign-source income derived by a citizen of Pakistan in a tax year who was not a resident individual in any of the four tax years preceding the tax year in which the individual became a resident is exempt from tax in the tax year in which the individual became resident and in the following tax year. Corroborated by PwC Worldwide Tax Summaries, last reviewed 24 August 2026.
source: Income Tax Ordinance consolidated to 30 June 2026, s.51(1); corroborated by PwC Worldwide Tax Summaries Pakistan
note: Tier 1 and tier 2 agree. This is the two-year landing window for a genuinely returning overseas Pakistani and belongs in Guide A next to s.51(2). Together they mean the moment of return, not the fact of residence, is what starts worldwide taxation biting on foreign income for a returning expatriate.

claim: s.107(2): 'Subject to section 109, where any agreement is made in accordance with sub-section (1), the agreement and the provisions made by notification for implementing the agreement shall, notwithstanding anything contained in any law for the time being in force, have effect in so far as they provide for at least one of the following: (a) relief from the tax payable under this Ordinance; (b) the determination of the Pakistan-source income of non-resident persons; (c) where all the operations of a business are not carried on within Pakistan, the determination of the income attributable to operations carried on within and outside Pakistan...'. The override is expressly made subject to s.109, the recharacterisation of income and deductions provision.
source: Income Tax Ordinance consolidated to 30 June 2026, s.107(2)
note: This is the statutory mechanism by which a treaty can displace s.82(d) and it should be quoted rather than paraphrased. Two cautions for Guide A. First, the override operates only 'in so far as' the agreement provides one of the listed things, so it is not a general supremacy clause. Second, it is subject to s.109. Note also that s.107 sits in Chapter VIII, the same anti-avoidance chapter as s.111, which is a neat structural point for both guides.

claim: FBR Circular No. 05 of 2022-Operations (Income Tax), C.No.6(9)S(IR-Operations)/2021, dated 30 August 2021, 'Foreign Remittances - Exemption', sets out the four conditions for s.111(4): '(a) the remitted amount is in foreign exchange; (b) the amount is remitted into Pakistan through normal banking channels; (c) the amount is encashed by a scheduled bank; and (d) a certificate of encashment is issued by the bank concerned.' The circular states these four conditions must be 'concomitantly fulfilled'.
source: FBR Circular No. 05 of 2022-Operations (Income Tax), paragraph 6
note: THE BEST SINGLE PRIMARY SOURCE FOR GUIDE B and it answers the 'what do I actually need' question in FBR's own words. The document names the certificate a 'certificate of encashment' / 'encashment certificate'. It ends 'All Circulars and instructions issued on the matter previously stand rescinded', so it is the operative FBR instruction on s.111(4). Signed by the Secretary (IR Operations). Note the file name says Circular 05 and the header says 'Circular No. 05 of 2022 - Operations' while the date is 30 August 2021: quote the number and date exactly as printed rather than reconciling them.

claim: The same circular directs FBR field formations to take a lenient view: 'it is clarified that all cases of claim of foreign remittances be disposed of by according lenient interpretation to the conditions stipulated in section 111(4) of the ITO, 2001. Moreover, in order to win the trust of the taxpayers and spare the public resources for more productive use elsewhere, all Departmental appeals filed on the stricto sensu interpretation of the law, be withdrawn immediately, and no further appeals be filed if on all fours of this clarification.' It reproduces SBP's position that remittances via money service businesses, exchange companies and money transfer operators such as Western Union, MoneyGram and Ria satisfy all four conditions, including SBP's statement that 'An encashment certificate is issued by bank that has received foreign exchange from abroad on behalf of the beneficiaries'.
source: FBR Circular No. 05 of 2022-Operations, paragraphs 7 to 10 and SBP table
note: Explains the ADMINISTRATIVE origin of the Finance Act 2022 Explanation to s.111(4): SBP and FBR settled the MSB/EC/MTO question by circular in 2021, and Parliament then wrote it into the statute in 2022. That is a genuinely useful narrative for the guide and it is fully sourced. The circular also records the institutional dispute, with IRS field formations refusing the concession for Western Union remittances relying on ITA No.794/LB of 2021, and FBR arguing MSBs are not 'scheduled banks' under s.2(m) and s.37(1) of the SBP Act 1956.

claim: FBR's own account of the s.111(4) cap history, in Circular No. 05: 'Up until 2015, there was no upper limit to avail exemption u/s 111(4) of the ITO, 2001. A limit of Rs.10 million was brought in 2018, which has, later on, been reduced to Rs.5 million vide Finance, Act, 2019.'
source: FBR Circular No. 05 of 2022-Operations, paragraph 6
note: CONTESTED AND MUST NOT BE PUBLISHED AS IS. This FBR account CONFLICTS with the footnotes in the consolidated Ordinance, which attribute the 'not exceeding five million Rupees in a tax year' wording to the Finance Act 2021 substitution, not to the Finance Act 2019. Both are tier 1. The Ordinance footnote is the better evidence because it is the amendment record attached to the text itself, and the circular's sentence is loose in a document whose purpose was not to trace the cap. The safe course for the guide is to state only what is not in dispute: the shield was once unlimited, a cap was introduced, and the cap is Rs 5 million today. Do not put a year on the cap's introduction without resolving this against the Finance Acts 2018 to 2021 directly. Recording as a live discrepancy rather than picking a side. | SUPERSEDED by s111-4-cap-history-resolved. RESOLVED. The apparent tier-1 conflict was our own reading error, not a conflict between sources: a footnote reproducing substituted text already contained the five million figure with its own nested footnotes. FBR Circular No. 05 was right. See s111-4-cap-was-added-CORRECTED.

claim: The circular records the FBR reference relying on the Supreme Court in Army Welfare Sugar Mills Ltd and Others v Federation of Pakistan, 1992 SCMR 1652, for two principles of exemption: '(a) the onus of proof is on the one who claims exemption, and (b) that a provision relating to grant of tax exemption is to be construed strictly against the person asserting and in favor of the taxing officer.'
source: FBR Circular No. 05 of 2022-Operations, paragraph 8
note: Useful and honest counterweight for Guide B: even with the lenient-interpretation instruction, the burden of proof sits on the taxpayer claiming the benefit. That is the practical reason the encashment certificate matters and should be obtained at the time, not years later. Note this is FBR quoting the case in its own reference; we have not read the judgment, so attribute it as cited in the circular.

claim: Section 109A of the Income Tax Ordinance 2001 (Controlled Foreign Company, inserted by the Finance Act 2018) attributes the income of a non-resident company to a resident shareholder even where no dividend is paid. All four conditions in s.109A(2) must be met: (a) resident persons hold, directly or indirectly, more than 50% of capital or voting rights, or a single resident holds more than 40%; (b) foreign tax paid is less than 60% of the tax that would be payable under the Ordinance; (c) the company does not derive active business income as defined in s.109A(3); and (d) its shares are not traded on a recognised stock exchange in its country of residence. Two de minimis rules cut it off: attributable income is treated as ZERO if the resident's capital or voting rights are less than 10% (s.109A(6)), and the CFC's income is treated as ZERO if it is less than PKR 10 million (s.109A(7)).
source: Income Tax Ordinance 2001 s.109A, consolidated to 30 June 2026
note: HIGH VALUE and widely misstated. A typical single-owner US LLC used as a genuine services business will often fail condition (c) because it DOES derive active business income, and a small one falls under the PKR 10m floor anyway. So CFC is a real risk for a passive/holding structure and frequently NOT triggered for an operating software business. s.109A(3) active income requires both: not more than 20% of income from dividend, interest, property, capital gains, royalty, supply to an associate, licensing of intangibles and holding of securities; AND principally deriving income under the head 'income from business'. s.109A(10) prevents double taxation on later receipt and s.109A(11) gives a credit for foreign tax on the dividend.

claim: Section 116A of the Income Tax Ordinance 2001 requires a foreign income and assets statement from every resident taxpayer BEING AN INDIVIDUAL with foreign income of at least USD 10,000 or foreign assets of at least USD 100,000. The obligation is on individuals only; it does not apply to companies. Penalty entry 1AAA of the s.182(1) table is 2 percent of the foreign income or value of the foreign assets for each year of default. Section 195A makes failure to comply with a Commissioner's notice under s.116A(2) an offence punishable with imprisonment up to one year or a fine up to PKR 50,000 or both.
source: Income Tax Ordinance 2001 ss.116A, 182(1) entry 1AAA, 195A, consolidated to 30 June 2026
note: Verified against the 30 June 2026 consolidation, so post-Finance Act 2026 vintage. The individual-only scope matters: a founder holding a US LLC personally has a s.116A duty, whereas the same holding inside his Pakistani company does not create one for the company. Note also s.195B, prosecution for enabling offshore tax evasion, up to seven years or PKR 5 million, which reaches advisers.

claim: Section 199(1) of the Companies Act 2017 prohibits a company from making any investment in an associated company or associated undertaking except under the authority of a SPECIAL RESOLUTION stating the nature, period, amount and terms of the investment. The Explanation defines investment to include equity, loans, advances and guarantees. Section 2(4)(b) defines associated companies and undertakings to include the case where 'one is the subsidiary of another', and the definition is not limited to companies incorporated in Pakistan. Section 199(4) requires a further special resolution for any increase or change; s.199(5) requires a register of such investments at the registered office; s.199(6) makes contravention an offence at level 3 on the standard scale with joint and several liability of directors to reimburse the company for loss.
source: Companies Act 2017 ss.2(4), 199
note: SECOND EXPOSURE that SBP material does not mention and most guides omit entirely. A Pakistani company funding its own foreign subsidiary is investing in an associated undertaking, so it needs a members' special resolution (three quarters), not merely a board resolution. Under s.199(2) a loan (rather than equity) to the subsidiary carries the further requirement of a written agreement and a return not less than the investing company's borrowing cost, with directors personally liable if it is not recovered.

claim: RESOLVED, superseding the contested record s111-4-cap-history-per-fbr. The s.111(4) cap history is: NO upper limit until 2018; a Rs 10 million cap introduced by the Finance Act 2018; reduced to Rs 5 million by the Finance Act 2019; and the sub-section then RESTRUCTURED by the Finance Act 2021, which carried the Rs 5 million figure forward unchanged. The Finance Act 2026 did not touch it, so Rs 5 million in a tax year stands for tax year 2027.
source: FBR Circular No. 05 of 2022-Operations paragraph 6, read with the s.111 footnotes in the Income Tax Ordinance consolidated to 30 June 2026
note: The apparent tier-1 conflict was a reading error on our side, not a conflict in the sources. The Ordinance footnote says the Finance Act 2021 SUBSTITUTED sub-section (4), and the substituted text it reproduces ALREADY CONTAINS 'not exceeding five million Rupees in a tax year' with its own nested footnote markers. So the 2021 Act re-cast the sub-section and inherited the figure; it did not introduce it. FBR's circular is correct that the Rs 10m to Rs 5m reduction was the Finance Act 2019. Lesson worth keeping: in these consolidations the text QUOTED INSIDE a footnote is the OLD version, and reading a figure there as newly introduced by the substituting Act is exactly backwards. The guide may now safely say the shield was uncapped until 2018 and has been Rs 5 million since 2019.

claim: Exceeding the Rs 5 million threshold does not make the remittance taxable of itself. It removes the s.111(4) protection, so the Commissioner may require the taxpayer to explain the nature and source of the amount under s.111(1); if the explanation is satisfactory there is no addition, and if it is not, the amount is included in income under 'Income from Other Sources' to the extent not adequately explained.
source: Income Tax Ordinance consolidated to 30 June 2026, s.111(1) and s.111(4)
note: Follows directly from the statutory text and is the precise correction Guide B needs. The popular framing 'remittances above Rs 5 million are taxed' is wrong: what is lost above the cap is the no-questions-asked protection, not a tax exemption, because s.111(4) never conferred one. Secondary coverage corroborates this reading, e.g. 'even if the amount of foreign remittance is more than Rs5 million in a tax year, the commissioner can only ask the source'.

claim: Para 3, Chapter 20 of the FE Manual provides that a Pakistan national resident in Pakistan who is or becomes the owner of foreign securities is permitted to hold or retain them PROVIDED he has acquired them in a manner not involving a breach or violation of the Foreign Exchange regulations. Holding is therefore lawful only if the acquisition was lawful. Para 3 also notes that under s.13(1)(a) FERA, taking or sending securities out of Pakistan without SBP permission is prohibited.
source: SBP FE Manual Chapter 20 Para 3, consolidated 11 Sep 2025
note: KEY REBUTTAL to the most common consultant claim, that funding a foreign entity from offshore earnings puts it outside SBP's reach because no money leaves Pakistan. The proviso is drafted around the lawfulness of the ACQUISITION, not around the route of the funds. Present the counter-argument fairly too: FERA s.5(2)(b) says s.5 does not render unlawful a payment made with foreign exchange received as salary or payment for services not arising from business in Pakistan, and Chapter 12 requires export proceeds to be repatriated in the first place. This is genuinely arguable and should be published as a contested point, not as a settled prohibition.
